claim: Homozygous TP53 deletion occurs in various types of human cancers at frequencies ranging from 1% to 15%.
source: Copy number data in various human tumors published in TCGA database (access through cBioPortal (http://www.cbioportal.org; accessed 18 Aug 2016) (Gao et al., 2013) show that homozygous TP53 genomic deletion occurs in various human cancers, at frequencies ranging from 1% to 15% (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by TCGA database analysis cited in the text (Gao et al., 2013) and referenced figures showing deletion frequencies.

claim: FXR2 undergoes concomitant deletion in most tumors carrying TP53 homozygous deletion.
source: One of the neighboring genes, FXR2, located around 100 kb downstream of TP53 at chromosome 17p13.1, undergoes concomitant deletion in most tumors carrying TP53 homozygous deletion with only a few exceptions (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from TCGA database analysis and visual evidence in Figure 1A and B showing co-deletion patterns.

claim: FXR2 is located approximately 100 kb downstream of TP53 at chromosome 17p13.1.
source: FXR2 (Fragile X-related Protein 2, also known as FXR2P), located 100 kb downstream of TP53, is also a neighboring gene of TP53 at chromosome 17p13.1.
evidence: The claim states a specific genomic location based on established knowledge of chromosome mapping.

claim: The majority of cancer cell lines carrying TP53 homozygous deletion also contain FXR2 deletion according to the CCLE database.
source: Consistently, in the CCLE database (Barretina et al., 2012), the majority of cancer cell lines carrying TP53 homozygous deletion also contain FXR2 deletion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the CCLE database cited (Barretina et al., 2012) and referenced figure.

claim: FXR2 single deletion is rarely observed in human tumors.
source: However, FXR2 single deletion is rarely observed in human tumors.
evidence: The claim is based on observation from database analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: In TP53/FXR2 co-deletion tumors, the copy number of FXR1 and FMR1 is largely unaltered.
source: In TP53/FXR2 co-deletion tumors, the copy number of FXR1 and FMR1 (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) is largely unaltered.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: FXR1 or FMR1 copy number gain is mutually exclusive with TP53/FXR2 deletion.
source: Of note, FXR1 or FMR1 copy number gain was also observed in tumors, although this wasmutually exclusive with TP53/FXR2 deletion (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis shown in referenced figures.

claim: Cancer cells with homozygous co-deletion of TP53 and FXR2 exhibit either absent or significantly lower mRNA and protein levels of p53 and FXR2.
source: Our data showed that cancer cells with homozygous co-deletion of TP53 and FXR2 exhibit either absent or significantly lower mRNA and protein levels of p53 and FXR2.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from q-RT-PCR and Western Blot assays mentioned in the text.

claim: Copy-number-normal and co-deleted cell lines have comparable FXR1 and FMR1 levels.
source: By contrast, the copy-number-normal and co-deleted cell lines have comparable FXR1 and FMR1 levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: FXR1 inhibition blocks cell proliferation in human cancer cells containing homozygous deletion of both TP53 and FXR2.
source: Here, we demonstrate that inhibition of the remaining family member FXR1 selectively blocks cell proliferation in human cancer cells containing homozygous deletion of both TP53 and FXR2 in a collateral lethality manner.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from cell proliferation assays presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: FXR1 inhibition selectively blocks cell proliferation in a collateral lethality manner.
source: Here, we demonstrate that inhibition of the remaining family member FXR1 selectively blocks cell proliferation in human cancer cells containing homozygous deletion of both TP53 and FXR2 in a collateral lethality manner.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and the concept of collateral lethality applied to the findings.

claim: FXR1 recruits transcription factor STAT1 or STAT3 to gene promoters at the chromatin interface.
source: Mechanistically, in addition to its RNA-binding function, FXR1 recruits transcription factor STAT1 or STAT3 to gene promoters at the chromatin interface and regulates transcription thus, at least partially, mediating cell proliferation.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq, ChIP-PCR, and ChIP-WB data showing FXR1 and STAT1/3 co-localization at gene promoters.

claim: FXR1 regulates transcription, at least partially mediating cell proliferation.
source: Mechanistically, in addition to its RNA-binding function, FXR1 recruits transcription factor STAT1 or STAT3 to gene promoters at the chromatin interface and regulates transcription thus, at least partially, mediating cell proliferation.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including ChIP-seq, RNA-seq, and functional assays.

claim: The fragile X gene family contains three mammalian members: FMR1, FXR1, and FXR2.
source: The fragile X gene family contains three mammalian members, including fragile X mental retardation protein FMR1 (also called as FMRP) and its structural homologs FXR1 and FXR2 (Siomi et al., 1993, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature (Siomi et al., 1993, 1995).

claim: FMR1, FXR1, and FXR2 are highly conserved in many species and share a high degree of sequence similarity in major functional domains.
source: These proteins are highly conserved in many species and share a high degree of sequence similarity in major functional domains, including tandem Tudor, KH and RGG box domains (Kirkpatrick et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to established literature (Kirkpatrick et al., 2001).

claim: FMR1, FXR1, and FXR2 all participate in RNA-binding, regulation of mRNA metabolism, ribosome-binding, and translation.
source: They all participate in RNA-binding, regulation of mRNA metabolism, ribosome-binding, and translation (Ascano et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2014; Darnell et al., 2001; Siomi et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: FMR1, FXR1, and FXR2 contain nuclear localization and nuclear export signals which allow them to be shuttled between cytoplasm and nucleus.
source: These proteins contain nuclear localization and nuclear export signals which allow them to be shuttled between cytoplasm and nucleus (Eberhart et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to established literature (Eberhart et al., 1996).

claim: FMR1 is highly expressed in neurons and plays a critical role in synaptic plasticity.
source: FMR1, which is highly expressed in neurons, plays a critical role in synaptic plasticity and its silencing results in Fragile X Syndrome, an inherited intellectual disability and the major cause of autism (Consortium, 1994; Darnell et al., 2011; Santoro et al., 2012; Verkerk et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Silencing of FMR1 results in Fragile X Syndrome, an inherited intellectual disability and the major cause of autism.
source: FMR1, which is highly expressed in neurons, plays a critical role in synaptic plasticity and its silencing results in Fragile X Syndrome, an inherited intellectual disability and the major cause of autism (Consortium, 1994; Darnell et al., 2011; Santoro et al., 2012; Verkerk et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: FXR1 is ubiquitously expressed and has potential roles in cardiac and skeletal muscle development.
source: FXR1 is ubiquitously expressed and has potential roles in cardiac and skeletal muscle development (Huot et al., 2005; Mientjes et al., 2004; Van't Padje et al., 2009; Whitman et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: FXR1 and FXR2 possess both common and distinct functions in post-transcriptional regulation.
source: Increasing evidence suggests that FXR1 and FXR2 possess both common and distinct functions in post-transcriptional regulation (Ascano et al., 2012; Cavallaro et al., 2008; Darnell et al., 2009; Say et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: FXR1 copy number was amplified and demonstrated oncogenic activity in lung squamous cell carcinoma.
source: FXR1 copy number was amplified and demonstrated oncogenic activity in lung squamous cell carcinoma (Comtesse et al., 2007; Qian et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Comtesse et al., 2007; Qian et al., 2015).

claim: FXR1 downregulates p21 by binding and reducing its mRNA stability and/or by modulating p53 expression to avoid senescence in cancer.
source: A recent study suggested that FXR1 downregulates p21 by binding and reducing its mRNA stability and/or by modulating p53 expression to avoid senescence in cancer (Majumder et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Majumder et al., 2016).

claim: All three members of the FMR1 family contain a tandem Tudor domain at the N-terminus belonging to the Royal family of chromatin-binding proteins.
source: At the N-terminus, all three members of the FMR1 family contain a tandem Tudor domain belonging to the Royal family of chromatin-binding proteins (Adams-Cioaba et al., 2010; Hu et al., 2015; Myrick et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: The tandem Tudor domain in FMR1 recognizes methylated lysine on histones at the chromatin interface.
source: The tandem Tudor domain in FMR1 was reported to recognize methylated lysine on histones at the chromatin interface, thus resulting in the protein's subsequent localization to the DNA damage loci, thereby facilitating the repair process (Adams-Cioaba et al., 2010; Alpatov et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Adams-Cioaba et al., 2010; Alpatov et al., 2014).

claim: The tandem Tudor domain in FMR1 facilitates localization to DNA damage loci and the repair process.
source: The tandem Tudor domain in FMR1 was reported to recognize methylated lysine on histones at the chromatin interface, thus resulting in the protein's subsequent localization to the DNA damage loci, thereby facilitating the repair process (Adams-Cioaba et al., 2010; Alpatov et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Adams-Cioaba et al., 2010; Alpatov et al., 2014).

claim: FXR1 inhibition only suppressed cell proliferation in cell lines with TP53/FXR2 co-deletion but not in copy-number-normal cells.
source: Consistently, FXR1 inhibition only suppressed cell proliferation in the cell lines with TP53/FXR2 co-deletion (H358, HL-60, KATOIII and KMS-11) but not in the copy-number-normal cells (AGS, A549, MKN45 and HepG2), as indicated in Figure 1C and also in Table 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from cell proliferation assays shown in Figure 1C, Table 1, and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Ectopic expression of shRNA-resistant FXR1 rescued the anti-proliferative phenotype induced by FXR1 inhibition.
source: In multiple cancer cell lines, the growth rate was recovered to a level comparable to that of the control, indicating that FXR1 inhibition was responsible for the growth phenotype (Figure 1—figure supplement 5, Figure 1D, Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental rescue data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Expression of FXR2 rescued the anti-proliferative phenotype induced by FXR1 inhibition, suggesting that FXR2 and FXR1 have redundant functions.
source: Consistent with the FXR1m data, expression of FXR2 also rescued the anti-proliferative phenotype induced by FXR1 inhibition, suggesting that FXR2 and FXR1 have redundant functions (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental rescue data shown in Figure 1D and inference from the results.

claim: Ectopic expression of FXR2 showed only partial rescue compared with FXR1m, suggesting that FXR1 and FXR2 may also have some distinct functions.
source: However, ectopic expression of FXR2 only showed partial rescue compared with FXR1m, suggesting that the proteins may also have some distinct functions.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental rescue data comparing FXR1 and FXR2.

claim: FMR1 did not rescue FXR1 knockdown-induced anti-proliferation.
source: Interestingly, FMR1 did not rescue FXR1 knockdown-induced anti-proliferation (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental rescue data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: FMR1 knockdown had no impact on proliferation in both TP53/FXR2 copy-number-normal and co-deleted cancer cells.
source: Furthermore, FMR1 knockdown had no impact on proliferation in both TP53/FXR2 copy-number-normal and co-deleted cancer cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: Dox-induced FXR1 downregulation significantly reduced tumor growth in the TP53/FXR2 co-deleted cell line HL-60-derived xenograft model.
source: Dox-induced FXR1 downregulation significantly reduced tumor growth in the TP53/FXR2 co-deleted cell line HL-60-derived xenograft model (Figure 1G), but had no impact on growth in the copy-number-normal cell A549-derived xenograft (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo xenograft data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: FXR1 downregulation had no impact on tumor growth in the copy-number-normal cell A549-derived xenograft.
source: Dox-induced FXR1 downregulation significantly reduced tumor growth in the TP53/FXR2 co-deleted cell line HL-60-derived xenograft model (Figure 1G), but had no impact on growth in the copy-number-normal cell A549-derived xenograft (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo xenograft data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: shRNA-induced FXR1 downregulation significantly inhibited cell proliferation only in the TP53 and FXR2 double knockout clones.
source: Consistent with the phenotypes observed in cancer cell lines, shRNA-induced FXR1 downregulation significantly inhibited cell proliferation only in the TP53 and FXR2 double knockout clones (Figure 2B) and had no effect on the TP53 single KO (Figure 2C) or FXR2 single KO (Figure 2D) clones.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from CRISPR-engineered cell clones shown in Figures 2B, 2C, and 2D.

claim: FXR1 downregulation had no effect on cell proliferation in TP53 single KO or FXR2 single KO clones.
source: Consistent with the phenotypes observed in cancer cell lines, shRNA-induced FXR1 downregulation significantly inhibited cell proliferation only in the TP53 and FXR2 double knockout clones (Figure 2B) and had no effect on the TP53 single KO (Figure 2C) or FXR2 single KO (Figure 2D) clones.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from CRISPR-engineered cell clones shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: Resistance to FXR1 inhibition in FXR2 single knockout clones and the FXR2 homozygous deletion cell line Hep3B suggested that p53 deficiency is required for FXR1 to function in regulating cell proliferation.
source: Resistance to FXR1 inhibition in both FXR2 single knockout clones (Figure 2D) and the FXR2 homozygous deletion cell line Hep3B (Figure 1E) suggested that p53 deficiency is required for FXR1 to function in regulating cell proliferation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data shown in Figures 2D and 1E.

claim: TP53 knockdown by siRNA enhanced cell growth in FXR2 KO cells.
source: In line with its tumor suppressor function, TP53 knockdown by siRNA enhanced cell growth in the tested cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: TP53 knockdown granted FXR1 the capability to regulate cell proliferation in FXR2 KO cells.
source: Interestingly, TP53 knockdown granted FXR1 the capability to regulate cell proliferation: diminished FXR1 suppressed the growth of TP53 siRNA-treated FXR2 KO cells but not of control siRNA-treated FXR2 KO cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Knockout of TP53 and FXR2 didn't change the expression of FXR1 or FMR1.
source: Moreover, knockout of TP53 and FXR2 didn't change the expression of FXR1 or FMR1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Knockdown of FXR2 upon Dox induction suppressed proliferation in TP53/FXR1 DKO clones.
source: We observed that knockdown of FXR2 upon Dox induction suppressed proliferation (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), further confirming the redundancy between FXR1 and FXR2.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The tandem Tudor domain is necessary for FXR1 to regulate cell proliferation.
source: These data indicate that the tandem Tudor domain is necessary for FXR1 to regulate cell proliferation.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from rescue assays with different FXR1 isoforms.

claim: Only the full-length FXR1_a could rescue FXR1 shRNA-induced anti-proliferation.
source: Interestingly, only the full-length (FXR1_a) could rescue FXR1 shRNA-induced anti-proliferation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental rescue data with different FXR1 isoforms.

claim: The Tudor-domain-truncated version FXR1_c completely lost its ability to rescue cell proliferation.
source: The Tudor-domain-truncated version FXR1_c completely lost its ability to rescue cell proliferation (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental rescue data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The Tudor domain of FXR1 showed binding to histone H3 containing methylated lysine at various positions, especially H3K4me1, H3K4me3, H3K9me3, H3K27me2, H3K36me1, and H3K79me2.
source: The Tudor domain showed binding to histone H3 containing methylated lysine at various positions, especially H3K4me1, H3K4me3, H3K9me3, H3K27me2, H3K36me1, and H3K79me2 (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from histone MLA pulldown assay shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The histone binding pattern of the tandem Tudor domain of FXR1 is similar to that of FMR1.
source: The histone binding pattern of the tandem Tudor domain of FXR1 is similar to that of FMR1.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of experimental data with known FMR1 binding patterns.

claim: FXR1 interacted with multiple proteins involved in chromatin and transcriptional signaling, including STAT1, STAT3, CHD4, SNF2H, histone H2B, H3K4me3, and DNA topoisomerase TOP2A.
source: In agreement with our DAVID enrichment analysis, FXR1 interacted with multiple proteins that are involved in chromatin and transcriptional signaling, including the transcription factors STAT1 and STAT3, the chromatin regulator CHD4, SNF2H, histone H2B and H3K4me3, and DNA topoisomerase TOP2A in H358 cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-WB data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Phosphorylated STAT1 or STAT3 can interact with FXR1.
source: We discovered that phosphorylated STAT1 or STAT3 can also interact with FXR1 from the ChIP-WB analysis in the same cells (Figure 4C, lower panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-WB data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: FXR1 may directly interact with both STAT1 and STAT3.
source: Importantly, the in vitro pull-down assay using the purified tagged proteins showed that FXR1 may directly interact with both STAT1 and STAT3 (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro pulldown assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: FXR1 had no impact on the phosphorylation of STAT1 or STAT3 or on their shuttling from the cytoplasm to the nucleus.
source: Interestingly, FXR1 had no impact on the phosphorylation of STAT1 or STAT3 or on their shuttling from the cytoplasm to the nucleus (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: FXR1 ChIP-seq peaks are primarily located at gene promoters close to transcriptional start sites (TSS).
source: We identified unfiltered 882 peaks of FXR1 (Supplementary file 3), primarily located at gene promoters close to transcriptional start sites (TSS) (Figure 5A–B and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figures 5A-B and Supplementary file 3.

claim: STAT1, STAT3 and H3K4me3 were also primarily located at TSS.
source: In agreement with our hypothesis, STAT1, STAT3 and H3K4me3 were also primarily located at TSS (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, and Supplementary file 3.

claim: The location of FXR1 significantly overlapped with those of STAT1, STAT3, and H3K4me3 at their target genes.
source: Interestingly, the location of FXR1 significantly overlapped with those of STAT1, STAT3, and H3K4me3 at their target genes (Figure 5C and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq overlap analysis shown in Figure 5C and Supplementary file 3.

claim: FXR1 peaks rarely overlap with H3K9me3 or H3K27me3, indicating FXR1's potential role in facilitating active transcription.
source: FXR1 peaks rarely overlap with H3K9me3 or H3K27me3 (for examples, see Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2, and Supplementary file 3), indicating FXR1's potential role in facilitating active transcription.
evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-seq data analysis and inference about transcriptional activity.

claim: Upon inducible FXR1 knockdown, genes ARID1A, CASC4, TRAPPC9, GLI1, CITED1, NPAS3, and SSBP2 were consistently downregulated in both H358 and KATOIII cells.
source: Upon inducible FXR1 knockdown, genes ARID1A, CASC4, TRAPPC9, GLI1, CITED1, NPAS3, and SSBP2 were consistently downregulated in both H358 and KATOIII cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by q-RT-PCR data from FXR1 knockdown experiments.

claim: FXR1 is located at the target gene promoters.
source: The promoter regions of the target gene were detected in the FXR1 ChIP pull-down complex, indicating that FXR1 is located at the target gene promoters (Figure 5F, shCtrl/Dox- and FXR1-sh3/Dox-).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: STAT1 or STAT3 were located in the vicinity of FXR1 at the target gene promoter.
source: Using the same approach, STAT1 or STAT3 were located in the vicinity of FXR1 at the target gene promoter (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: FXR1 knockdown resulted in STAT1 and STAT3 eviction from the gene promoters.
source: More interestingly, FXR1 knockdown resulted in STAT1 and STAT3 eviction from the gene promoters (Figure 5F), suggesting that FXR1 is required to recruit or stabilize STAT1 and STAT3 at gene promoters.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: FXR1 is required to recruit or stabilize STAT1 and STAT3 at gene promoters.
source: More interestingly, FXR1 knockdown resulted in STAT1 and STAT3 eviction from the gene promoters (Figure 5F), suggesting that FXR1 is required to recruit or stabilize STAT1 and STAT3 at gene promoters.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from ChIP-PCR data showing STAT eviction upon FXR1 knockdown.

claim: STAT3 did not affect FXR1's occupancy of sites at gene promoters.
source: On the other hand, STAT3 did not affect FXR1's occupancy of sites at gene promoters because its knockdown had no effect on the localization of FXR1 at promoters (Figure 5G, Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: FXR1 peak-associated genes had 89.95% overlap with FXR2 peak-associated genes in AGS cells.
source: FXR1 peak-associated genes had 89.95% (2935/3263 FXR1-peak-associated genes) overlap with FXR2 peak-associated genes in AGS cells (Figure 5I), and this percentage increased when we focused on TSS (Figure 5—figure supplement 4B and Supplementary file 3), suggesting a shared function of FXR1 and FXR2 at gene promoters.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq overlap analysis shown in Figure 5I and Supplementary file 3.

claim: FXR1 and FXR2 share a function at gene promoters.
source: FXR1 peak-associated genes had 89.95% (2935/3263 FXR1-peak-associated genes) overlap with FXR2 peak-associated genes in AGS cells (Figure 5I), and this percentage increased when we focused on TSS (Figure 5—figure supplement 4B and Supplementary file 3), suggesting a shared function of FXR1 and FXR2 at gene promoters.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from ChIP-seq overlap data.

claim: There was significant overlap between FXR1-associated genes and STAT1/3-associated genes in AGS cells.
source: There was also significant overlapbetween FXR1-associated genes and STAT1/3-associated genes, suggesting at least partially, that FXR1 mediates STAT1/3 transcriptional activity in AGS cells (Figure 5I, Figure 5—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq overlap analysis shown in Figure 5I and Figure 5—figure supplement 4B.

claim: FXR1 mediates STAT1/3 transcriptional activity, at least partially.
source: There was also significant overlapbetween FXR1-associated genes and STAT1/3-associated genes, suggesting at least partially, that FXR1 mediates STAT1/3 transcriptional activity in AGS cells (Figure 5I, Figure 5—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from ChIP-seq overlap data.

claim: The expression levels of target genes remained constant after FXR2 knockdown except for a slight inhibition of CASC4 and TRAPPC9 expression.
source: Furthermore, the expression levels of target genes remained constant after FXR2 knockdown except for a slight inhibition of CASC4 and TRAPPC9 expression, further confirming the redundant function shared by FXR1 and FXR2 (Figure 5J, lower panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by q-RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: Only a small portion of STAT1/3 peaks in the genome (0.7–1.57%) overlap with FXR1 peaks in H358 cells.
source: Our study showed that only a small portion of STAT1/3 peaks in the genome (0.7–1.57%) overlap with FXR1 peaks, indicating that FXR1 cooperates with STAT1/3 in a small number of STAT target genes' transcription in H358 cells (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq overlap analysis in Supplementary file 3.

claim: 24.38–25.74% of FXR1 peaks overlap with STAT1 and STAT3 peaks, suggesting a significant role for STATs in FXR1's transcriptional activity.
source: By contrast, 24.38–25.74% of FXR1 peaks overlap with STAT1 and STAT3 peaks, suggesting a significant role for STATs in FXR1's transcriptional activity (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-seq overlap analysis and inference about functional significance.

claim: The JAK inhibitor S-Ruxolitinib suppressed STAT1 phosphorylation in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Indeed, we found that the JAK inhibitor S-Ruxolitinib suppressed STAT1 phosphorylation in a dose-dependent manner and inhibited the expression of some but not all FXR1 target genes in H358 cells (Figure 5K, Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: The JAK inhibitor S-Ruxolitinib inhibited the expression of some but not all FXR1 target genes in H358 cells.
source: Indeed, we found that the JAK inhibitor S-Ruxolitinib suppressed STAT1 phosphorylation in a dose-dependent manner and inhibited the expression of some but not all FXR1 target genes in H358 cells (Figure 5K, Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by q-RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5K and Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: JAK inhibitor didn't suppress FXR1 expression.
source: Note that JAK inhibitor didn't suppress FXR1 expression (Figure 5K).
evidence: The claim is supported by q-RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: Among the genes whose promoters are occupied by FXR1, 45 out of 210 genes showed regulation upon FXR1 knockdown in RNA-seq assay.
source: Among the genes whose promoters are occupied by FXR1, 45 out of 210 genes showed regulation upon FXR1 knockdown in RNA-seq assay (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and Supplementary file 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and Supplementary file 7.

claim: Knockdown of GLI1 showed the most consistent anti-proliferative effect among the seven target genes tested.
source: Among the seven target genes, knockdown of GLI1 showed the most consistent anti-proliferative effect whereas ARID1A, CITED1, or SSBP2 knockdown showed less inhibitory effect in a 7-day proliferation assay (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell proliferation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The combined knockdown of both the target genes and FXR1 showed an additive effect on cell growth inhibition.
source: As shown in the cell image and MTS detection (Figure 6A), the combined knockdown of both the target genes and FXR1 showed an additive effect on cell growth inhibition.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell proliferation data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: GLI1 downregulation by siRNA showed the most dramatic combinatorial effect with FXR1 knockdown in suppressing cell proliferation.
source: Amongst the target genes, GLI1 downregulation by siRNA showed the most dramatic combinatorial effect with FXR1 knockdown in suppressing cell proliferation.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell proliferation data from combinatorial knockdown experiments.

claim: FXR1 knockdown induced the cleavage of PARP in H358 cells.
source: Following this lead, we found that FXR1 knockdown induced the cleavage of PARP in H358 cells (Figure 6B), a signal event of cell apoptosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: FXR1 inhibition increased caspase 3/7 activity.
source: Furthermore, FXR1 inhibition increased caspase 3/7 activity (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by caspase activity assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Knockdown of FXR1 target gene GLI1 induced apoptotic signals including the cleavage of PARP and activation of caspase 3/7.
source: Consistently, knockdown of FXR1 target gene GLI1 also induced apoptotic signals including the cleavage of PARP and activation of caspase 3/7 in the same cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot and caspase activity assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The effect on PARP cleavage could be rescued by ectopic expression of shRNA-resistant full-length FXR1m_a, indicating a direct role of FXR1 in cell apoptosis signaling.
source: More interestingly, the effect on PARP cleavage could be rescued by ectopic expression of shRNA-resistant full-length FXR1m_a, indicating a direct role of FXR1 in cell apoptosis signaling (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Downregulation of FXR1 inhibits cell growth through the activation of cell apoptotic signaling, at least partially through regulating target gene transcription.
source: These data suggest that downregulation of FXR1 inhibits cell growth through the activation of cell apoptotic signaling, at least partially through regulating target gene transcription.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results showing apoptosis induction and target gene regulation.

claim: Inhibition of FXR1 is a potential therapeutic approach to targeting human cancers harboring TP53 homozygous deletion.
source: Our study anticipates that inhibition of FXR1 is a potential therapeutic approach to targeting human cancers harboring TP53 homozygous deletion.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about therapeutic potential derived from the study's findings.

claim: p53 primarily serves as a transcription factor to control various cellular stress-response signaling pathways, including cell cycle arrest, DNA repair, senescence and apoptosis.
source: p53, a critical tumor suppressor, primarily serves as a transcription factor to control various cellular stress-response signaling pathways, including cell cycle arrest, DNA repair, senescence and apoptosis (Vousden and Lane, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to established literature (Vousden and Lane, 2007).

claim: Loss of p53 function through mutation or deletion of TP53 is a common feature in a majority of human cancers.
source: Loss of p53 function through mutation or deletion of its encoding TP53 is a common feature in a majority of human cancers, resulting in the escape from tumor-suppressor activities.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in cancer biology.

claim: Tumor suppressor genes are often inactivated by genomic deletions that encompass the deletion of neighboring genes.
source: In cancer, tumor suppressor genes are often inactivated by genomic deletions that encompass the deletion of neighboring genes.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in cancer genetics.

claim: Bystander genes often belong to multigene families and their deletion is tolerated due to genetic redundancy.
source: Such bystander genes often belong to multigene families; therefore, their deletion is tolerated due to genetic redundancy.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about genetic redundancy.

claim: The 'collateral lethality' concept suggests that passenger deletion predisposes cancer cells to vulnerabilities induced by further inhibition of the remaining genes in the family.
source: The newly proposed 'collateral lethality' concept suggests that such passenger deletion predisposes cancer cells to vulnerabilities that are induced by further inhibition of the remaining genes in the family, whose functions are essential and redundant (Muller et al., 2012, 2015; Nijhawan et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Muller et al., 2012, 2015; Nijhawan et al., 2012).

claim: Inhibition of POLR2A was demonstrated in colorectal cancers containing TP53 heterozygous deletion.
source: Drugging TP53-deleted cancers had been a challenging task until a recent report demonstrated inhibition of a neighboring gene POLR2A, which is located about 200 kb downstream of TP53 on chromosome 17 and undergoes heterozygous deletion in colorectal cancers containing TP53 heterozygous deletion (Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Liu et al., 2015).

claim: POLR2A is located about 200 kb downstream of TP53 on chromosome 17.
source: Drugging TP53-deleted cancers had been a challenging task until a recent report demonstrated inhibition of a neighboring gene POLR2A, which is located about 200 kb downstream of TP53 on chromosome 17 and undergoes heterozygous deletion in colorectal cancers containing TP53 heterozygous deletion (Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on established genomic location information cited from literature (Liu et al., 2015).

claim: Homozygous deletion occurs less frequently and is more focal than heterozygous deletion.
source: Homozygous deletion, resulting in inactivation of both alleles, occurs less frequently and is more focal than heterozygous deletion.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in cancer genetics.

claim: There is no documented therapeutic strategy targeting homozygous TP53-deleted cancers.
source: There is no documented therapeutic strategy targeting homozygous TP53-deleted cancers.
evidence: The claim is based on the state of knowledge at the time of the study.

claim: POLR2A is co-deleted in a majority of tumors with TP53 homozygous deletion.
source: POLR2A is co-deleted in a majority of tumors with TP53 homozygous deletion, and thus its inhibition would not be relevant.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from database analysis.

claim: FXR2 belongs to the fragile X gene family that has essential functions in binding and regulating mRNA stability, transportation and translation.
source: It belongs to the fragile X gene family that has essential functions in binding and regulating mRNA stability, transportation and translation (Ascano et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2014; Darnell et al., 2001; Siomi et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: FXR1 binds to the mRNA of target genes such as CASC4, TRAPPC9, GLI1, and SSBP2.
source: Furthermore, we confirmed ChIP-MS findings and discovered that FXR1 binds to the mRNA of target genes such as CASC4, TRAPPC9, GLI1, and SSBP2 in the mRNA binding assays (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by mRNA binding assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: FXR1 has dynamic functions in transcription and subsequent mRNA processing.
source: This raises the possibility that FXR1 has dynamic functions in transcription and subsequent mRNA processing.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation from the combined findings of transcriptional and RNA-binding functions.

claim: FXR1 knockout mice die shortly after birth.
source: The observation that FXR1 knockout mice die shortly after birth and knockdown of FXR1 causes abnormalities in striated muscle and heart in zebrafish (Mientjes et al., 2004; Zarnescu and Gregorio, 2013) raise potential safety concerns with regard to inhibiting FXR1 in cancer patients.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Mientjes et al., 2004; Zarnescu and Gregorio, 2013).

claim: Knockdown of FXR1 causes abnormalities in striated muscle and heart in zebrafish.
source: The observation that FXR1 knockout mice die shortly after birth and knockdown of FXR1 causes abnormalities in striated muscle and heart in zebrafish (Mientjes et al., 2004; Zarnescu and Gregorio, 2013) raise potential safety concerns with regard to inhibiting FXR1 in cancer patients.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Mientjes et al., 2004; Zarnescu and Gregorio, 2013).

claim: Concomitant deletion of passenger FXR2 in TP53-deleted cancer cells makes cell growth dependent on FXR1.
source: The recent discovery of the collateral lethality concept prompted us to hypothesize that concomitant deletion of passenger FXR2 in TP53-deleted cancer cells might make cell growth dependent on FXR1.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the collateral lethality concept and tested experimentally in the study.

claim: Concomitant deletion of FXR2 and TP53 is necessary for triggering FXR1 inhibition-induced cell lethality.
source: In the tested cell lines, the proliferation rate was unaltered (Figure 1F), suggesting that concomitant deletion of FXR2 and TP53 is necessary for triggering FXR1 inhibition-induced cell lethality.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing no effect in single deletion cell lines.

claim: Using an arbitrary 30% proliferation inhibition as a cut off, there was a clear pattern of FXR1 regulation of cell proliferation in TP53 and FXR2 co-deleted cancer cells.
source: Using an arbitrary 30% proliferation inhibition as a cut off, there was a clear pattern of FXR1 regulation of cell proliferation in TP53 and FXR2 co-deleted cancer cells.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of experimental data summarized in Table 1.

claim: 22% of FXR1 ChIP-seq peaks are enriched at promoter regions (defined as 5000 bp upstream and 1000 bp downstream of TSS).
source: 22% of peaks are enriched at promoter regions (defined as 5000 bp upstream and 1000 bp downstream of TSS) (p<1×e−5).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A total of 210 peak-associated genes were identified for FXR1 at TSS.
source: At TSS, a total of 210 peak-associated genes were identified for FXR1 (Figure 5C and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5C and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Among FXR1 TSS-associated genes, 145, 147 and 200 peak-associated genes overlapped with STAT1, STAT3 and H3K4me3, respectively.
source: Among them, 145, 147 and 200 peak-associated genes overlapped with STAT1, STAT3 and H3K4me3, respectively (Figure 5C and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq overlap analysis shown in Figure 5C and Supplementary file 3.

claim: JAK inhibition had no effect on inhibiting cancer cell proliferation in FXR1 shRNA-sensitive cells.
source: Although JAK inhibition suppressed the expression of some FXR1 target genes, it had no effect on inhibiting cancer cell proliferation in FXR1 shRNA-sensitive cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell proliferation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 6.

claim: p53 deficiency may augment FXR1's role in transcription regulation in controlling cancer cell proliferation.
source: Considering that FXR1 can both suppress p53 to escape senescence (Majumder et al., 2016) and activate gene transcription (evidence from this study), p53 deletion may augment FXR1's role in transcription regulation in controlling cancer cell proliferation.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation combining findings from this study and cited literature.

claim: FXR1 copy number gain occurs in some types of cancers, particularly in lung squamous carcinoma, and its occurrence is mutually exclusive with TP53 and FXR2 homozygous deletion.
source: FXR1 copy number gain occurs in some types of cancers, particularly in lung squamous carcinoma (Comtesse et al., 2007; Qian et al., 2015) and its occurrence is mutually exclusive with TP53 and FXR2 homozygous deletion according to TCGA database (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by database analysis and citations to published studies.

claim: FXR1 controls tumor growth in cancers with either TP53/FXR2 homozygous deletion or FXR1 amplification.
source: Together with our study, this evidence suggests that FXR1 controls tumor growth in cancers with either TP53/FXR2 homozygous deletion or FXR1 amplification.
evidence: The claim is based on inference combining findings from this study with published literature.

claim: FXR1 may cooperate with other transcription factors in regulating transcription, such as BTF.
source: FXR1 may also cooperate with other transcription factors in regulating transcription; examples include BTF (Ma et al., 2014) which was also identified in an FXR1 protein complex in our ChIP-MS study.
evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-MS data and citation to published literature (Ma et al., 2014).

claim: FXR1 interacts with several proteins that have essential function in transcription regulation, including TOP2A/2B, GTF2A, and FACT80.
source: In addition, we identified several other FXR1-interacting proteins that have essential function in transcription regulation, including TOP2A/2B, GTF2A, and FACT80.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-MS data identifying these protein interactions.

claim: FXR1 binds to and regulates mRNA processing and translation.
source: Our ChIP-MS data confirmed the established role of FXR1, which binds to and regulates mRNA processing and translation (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-MS data shown in Figure 4B and established knowledge.

claim: FXR1 binds to some but not all of its target gene mRNAs, which may contribute to its role in proliferation regulation.
source: Our study confirmed that, in addition to its direct function in transcription, FXR1 binds to some but not all of its target gene mRNAs, which may contribute to its role in proliferation regulation.
evidence: The claim is based on mRNA binding assay data and inference about functional contribution.
